notes.meaning: Pilate ordered his soldiers to whip Jesus. Roman floggings were very harsh, far worse than the Jewish limit of forty lashes. Pilate hoped this lesser punishment would satisfy the crowd so he could let Jesus go. Christians have long seen Isaiah 53:5 here: the innocent one took the blows we deserved, and 'by his wounds we are healed.'

The soldiers turned Jesus into a joke king. They wove thorns into a crown and threw a purple robe on him, since purple was the color of kings. Then they kept coming up to 'honor' him while slapping his face. Matthew Henry points out that Jesus quietly bore both the pain and the shame for our sake.

Pilate went back outside to the crowd. Once more he said he found nothing Jesus had done wrong. The same judge who later condemned Jesus first declared him innocent. Calvin says this shows Jesus was punished for other people's sins, not his own.

Jesus came out beaten and bleeding, dressed as a mock king. Pilate said, 'Here is the man!' He probably hoped the sight would stir pity. He also wanted to show how silly it was to fear this man as a dangerous rebel. Matthew Henry invites us to look at Jesus in his suffering with faith, and to love him.

The sight only made the chief priests and temple officers angrier, and they shouted for crucifixion. Pilate replied, 'You take him and crucify him.' He knew they could not legally do it. It was his frustrated way of saying he would not do their dirty work, because he still believed Jesus was innocent.

Now the leaders named their real complaint. Jesus had claimed to be the Son of God. To them that was blasphemy, which means speaking as if you were God. Their law punished it with death (Leviticus 24:16). Calvin says the rule itself was right, since no mere man may claim God's honor. Their mistake was that Jesus truly is the Son of God, and they never honestly looked into it.

This made Pilate even more afraid. He already feared shedding innocent blood, and his wife had warned him about a dream. Romans told stories of gods visiting earth in human form. So Pilate may have wondered whether Jesus was more than a man.

Pilate took Jesus back inside his headquarters and asked, 'Where are you from?' He already knew Jesus came from Galilee. He was really asking whether Jesus was human or divine. Jesus stayed silent, as Isaiah 53:7 foretold of the lamb led to slaughter. He had already explained his kingdom, and he had not come to plead for his release but to suffer in our place.

The silence stung Pilate's pride. He boasted that Jesus' life was in his hands. Matthew Henry and Calvin point out the irony: Pilate had called Jesus innocent, yet bragged that he could crucify him. No ruler truly has the right to do wrong.

Jesus reminded Pilate that his power came 'from above,' that is, from God. Paul teaches the same truth in Romans 13:1. Pilate was only a tool within God's plan, and he would answer to God for how he used his power. Pilate still sinned, but the one who handed Jesus over sinned more. Most commentators think this means Caiaphas the high priest, sometimes along with Judas and the Jewish council, who acted with more knowledge and out of hatred.

After this, Pilate tried even harder to free Jesus. But the leaders played their strongest card. They said that freeing a man who called himself king would make Pilate disloyal to Caesar. 'Friend of Caesar' was a name for the emperor's trusted officials. The emperor Tiberius was very suspicious, and Pilate feared being reported to him.

That threat broke Pilate's resolve. He brought Jesus out and sat on the judge's seat to give the official sentence. The place was a raised spot paved with stones, called Gabbatha, which means a high place. Calvin sees a picture here: Christ was condemned from a high seat so that he, the true Judge from heaven, may clear us on the last day.

It was the day of Preparation, the Friday before the Sabbath of Passover week. John says it was 'about the sixth hour.' Mark says Jesus was crucified at the third hour, so commentators explain the times in different ways. Some say John counts hours the Roman way, from midnight, which makes it about 6 a.m. Others think a copyist mixed up two Greek letters that looked alike. Pilate's 'Here is your King!' was biting sarcasm aimed at the leaders.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic commentator Cornelius à Lapide reports a view that Pilate gave in at the third hour and then formally passed sentence at the sixth.

notes.meaning: The crowd screamed, 'Away with him!' Pilate mocked them: 'Shall I crucify your King?' The chief priests answered, 'We have no king but Caesar.' With those words they gave up Israel's old belief that God was their King, and their hope of the Messiah, the Savior-King God had promised. Calvin calls this madness, because by rejecting Christ they cut themselves off from God's blessing. They were also pretending to be loyal to a Roman ruler they hated.

Then Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified. John uses the same word for 'handed over' that described the leaders handing Jesus to Pilate. Pilate gave in because fear of people outweighed his fear of God. Matthew Henry adds that Christ was condemned so that those who trust in him would never be condemned.

Jesus carried his own cross, as condemned men were made to do. It was most likely the crossbeam, not the whole cross. The other Gospels tell how Simon of Cyrene later helped him when he grew weak. Jesus went outside the city to Golgotha, 'the Place of the Skull.' Calvin notes that offerings for sin were carried outside the camp, and Jesus suffered outside the gate as the sacrifice for our sins.

They nailed Jesus to the cross between two robbers, with him in the middle, as if he were the worst of the three. This fulfilled Isaiah 53:12: 'he was numbered with the transgressors,' meaning he was counted among lawbreakers. Calvin says all of this happened within God's plan. It shows both how seriously God takes sin and how great his love for us is.

Pilate wrote a sign for the cross naming Jesus' 'crime': JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. He meant it as a jab at the Jewish leaders. But God was guiding his pen. The 'charge' named no real crime, and it announced the truth that Jesus is King.

The cross stood near the city, so many people read the sign. It was written in Hebrew, the local language; in Latin, the official language of Rome; and in Greek, the language most people shared. Matthew Henry and Calvin see a hint here that Jesus would be made known as Savior to all nations, each in its own language.

The chief priests hated the sign. They wanted it changed to say only that Jesus claimed to be king. They felt rebuked by it, and they did not want their nation shamed. Robertson notes they feared the joke was on them, not on Jesus, and they were right.
